Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=9(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f=9{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=18u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =18u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =18\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The acceleration $a(t)$ of the particle is given by the derivative of the velocity with respect to time. Find the function $a(t).$

$a(t)=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \operatorname{cot}t$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write

$$
v(t)=4{csc}^{2}(t).
$$

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
v=4{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{csc}t.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=8u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{'}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =8u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =(8\operatorname{csc}t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =-8{csc}^{2}t\operatorname{cot}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express
\[
f(x) = -2(\sin{(x)})^{3}.
\]

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function
\[
f = -2u^{3}, \qquad u = \sin{(x)}.
\]

Differentiating, we get
\[
\dfrac{\textrm df}{\textrm d u} = -6u^2, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \cos{(x)}.
\]

We now apply the chain rule, and get
\begin{align*}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt]

& = -6u^2 \cdot \cos{(x)}\\[5pt]

&=\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-6\sin^2{(x)}\cos{(x)}}.
\end{align*}

First, we express

$$
f(x)=\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f=u^{3},\qquad u=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=3 u^{2},\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- \sin{\left(x \right)}.

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\\&=(3 u^{2})\cdot(- \sin{\left(x \right)})\\&=- 3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x)=- 9 \csc^{3}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=- 27 u^{2},\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- \cot{\left(x \right)} \csc{\left(x \right)}.

$$

$$
